title: Orla and the Puffin's Peak Quest
markdown:
The wind in the highlands was a boisterous fellow, always messing with Orla’s hair and scattering her potions. Orla, a witch who was both quietly capable and wonderfully eccentric, lived in a cottage that clung to the cliffside like a stubborn barnacle. Her walls were covered in dried herbs, shimmering crystals, and the occasional, slightly singed, tapestry. Her garden was less an orderly patch of greenery and more an experiment in unusual gardening, bursting with oddly shaped vegetables and flowers that glowed softly at dusk. Her only constant companions, apart from the whispers of magic that seemed to weave themselves into the air and the gusts that threatened her chimney, were Cobble, a donkey with legendary patience and an even more legendary grumble. Cobble had witnessed Orla’s magic firsthand, from the time she accidentally turned the milk blue (which surprisingly tasted like blueberries) to the time she levitated her entire sock drawer (a process that took a ridiculous amount of effort to reverse).

Today, however, Orla’s usual happy confusion was replaced by a mild, but very firm, frustration. Percival, her pet puffin, a creature of very particular tastes and incredibly inconvenient habits, had vanished. He wasn’t just hiding in the garden shed, which he usually did when he disapproved of her breakfast tea. Percival had disappeared into the most inconvenient place imaginable: the snow-covered passes of the Whispering Peaks. This was a place where the wind could carve ice sculptures out of solid rock and avalanches were as common as sheep down in the meadows.

“Cobble,” Orla said, pushing her spectacles back up her nose, a constant battle whenever she was deep in thought or a strong gust decided to test their grip. “Percival has, I believe, developed a sudden and rather alarming interest in how ice changes mountains. Or perhaps he’s decided to personally check the stability of the highest crags.”

Cobble, who was trying to groom a particularly stubborn thistle from his mane with the air of someone utterly fed up with prickly situations, let out a long suffering sigh that sounded like a very old balloon slowly deflating. “Ice changes mountains, Orla? Or did he just see a shiny bit of ice reflecting the sun and decide to test your commitment to getting back your pet with a side of extreme weather? Knowing Percival, it’s probably the latter. He has a flair for the dramatic, that bird.”

Orla offered a small knowing smile that crinkled the corners of her eyes. “Exactly. That’s why we must venture forth. He always picks the most dramatic, yet somehow completely logical, escape routes. It’s his way of keeping us on our toes, I suspect. A puffin’s work is never done, as they say. Or at least, he thinks so.”

And so, with a satchel of carefully packed, slightly alarming herbs that smelled vaguely of old parchment and dried regret, and a thermos of strong lukewarm tea that tasted remarkably like courage and slightly burnt toast, Orla mounted Cobble. The snow lay in thick pristine blankets, muffling the usual sounds of the highlands. Ancient pine trees stood like dark silent sentinels, their branches bowed under winter’s frosty weight. Scattered villages clung to the sheer rock faces, their windows like tiny watchful eyes, hinting at lives lived in defiance of the elements.

Their journey into the higher passes was a study in contrasts. Orla, ever observant, pointed out the delicate frost patterns on an ancient fir branch that looked like intricate lace woven by frost fairies. Cobble, meanwhile, navigated the treacherous snowdrifts with a weary expertise, his hooves finding purchase where Orla imagined only solid ice should be. It was then, as the silence of the mountains seemed to deepen, that they heard it — a faint rhythmic thrumming, like a distant heartbeat, but with an unsettling vibrato that hinted at something more powerful.

“Hold, Orla,” a voice chirped, light as a falling snowflake and carrying an unusual clarity. “That is not a heartbeat. That is the song of the snow beginning to shift. A tune that can quickly turn into a rather unpleasant crescendo.”

A small elf, with hair the colour of spun moonlight and eyes that held the deep clear blue of a winter sky, emerged from behind a snow-laden pine. He wore boots that seemed to tread on air, leaving no imprint on the powdery surface. He had an air of gentle authority about him, like a very polite librarian who also happened to know where all the secret passages were. “Pip, at your service,” he said with a slight bow that was more a graceful inclination of his head. “And the mountains are talking. It’s always best to listen when they have something to say.”

“You can hear avalanches?” Orla asked, her witchy curiosity piqued. Her own senses were finely tuned, but this was something different, something more elemental.

“Before they even think about it,” Pip confirmed, his voice carrying a matter-of-fact tone that belied the extraordinary nature of his ability. “It’s a gift. Or a curse, depending on how much you enjoy spontaneous downhill travel. And believe me, a puffin making a bid for freedom is usually a clue that something more is afoot. Now, where are we off to, and what brings such discerning company into the higher passes on such a day?”

Orla, with a sigh that was more amused than weary, explained about Percival, the discerning puffin with a flair for the dramatic and an uncanny knack for finding the most inaccessible places. Pip’s ears, which were slightly pointed and seemed to move independently, twitched. “A puffin? In the Peaks? Intriguing. He’ll need a truly spectacular hiding place to warrant such an adventure. He’s not the sort to settle for a mere snowdrift, I’d wager. Follow me. The snow tells me the best routes, and the wind whispers secrets, but it’s the very bones of the mountain that hum the warnings. And sometimes, they hum about the whereabouts of adventurous birds.”

As they followed Pip, his tiny almost weightless steps leaving barely a trace, the air grew colder, and the landscape became more stark, carved by wind and ice into dramatic shapes. Suddenly a cacophony of crackling energy and flamboyant light erupted from a small sheltered ravine just off their path. Two figures, cloaked in swirling iridescent fabrics that shimmered with an unnatural light, were locked in a duel. It wasn’t a duel of earnest combat, but one of pure unadulterated showmanship.

“Ten points for the shimmering aura, Zephyr. Simply divine,” boomed a voice that echoed with theatrical resonance.

“And ten for your perfectly executed, yet remarkably derivative, ice shard volley, Gale,” retorted another voice, dripping with a practiced sarcastic sweetness. “Though I must say, the trajectory lacked a certain… artistic flourish. Mine, on the other hand,” — a shower of sapphire-blue ice crystals erupted from Gale’s outstretched hand, arcing in a perfect spiral — “were pure poetry.”

Pip sighed, a small puff of white mist escaping his lips. “Ah, Zephyr and Gale. The Style Council of Sorcery. They judge each other on flair and finesse. They once had a duel that lasted three days, solely over who could make their magical sparks more aesthetically pleasing. The local squirrels are still talking about the residual glitter.”

Orla watched, a small amused smile playing on her lips. She found their dedication to such frivolous displays rather endearing, in a way. “They seem… enthusiastically focused,” she commented, her voice low. “One might almost say they are lost in their own world.”

Cobble snorted, a sound that vibrated through his sturdy frame. “They’re showing off. Percival would find them tiresome. Too much noise, not enough substance. He prefers a quiet appreciation of fine craftsmanship, not a fireworks display.”

“Indeed,” Orla agreed, her eyes twinkling. “But perhaps their dazzling displays have… distracted something. Or someone. Pip, you said the snow was humming about Percival and something loud and bright?”

Pip, meanwhile, was sniffing the air, his nose twitching like a curious rabbit’s. He closed his eyes for a moment, his pointed ears swiveling. “The snow tells me… Percival is not far. And he’s near something… loud. And brightly coloured. Very, very brightly coloured. It’s a rather unusual combination, even for these mountains.”

Following Pip’s intuition and Orla’s keen observation of a peculiar shimmer in the otherwise uniform white of the snow-laden ravine — a shimmer that didn’t quite belong, a sort of misplaced sparkle — they cautiously approached. Zephyr and Gale, completely absorbed in their magical one-upmanship, hadn’t noticed them. And there, perched precariously on a narrow ledge just above their heads, looking utterly unimpressed by the whole spectacle, was Percival. He had, Orla realized with a silent chuckle that vibrated through her bones, somehow fashioned a rather cozy-looking nest out of discarded shimmering spell components. These were the very materials Zephyr and Gale were so proud of, the source of their gaudy glittery displays. Percival, it seemed, had decided to redecorate.

Percival gave a rather disgruntled squawk, a sound that cut through the crackle of magic like a sharp whistle. He clearly felt the duel was interfering with his carefully curated ambiance. His magnificent new nest, made from what looked suspiciously like discarded moonbeams and bottled starlight, was being threatened by stray ice shards and excessive glitter.

Orla, with a quiet word and a gentle beckoning gesture, coaxed Percival down. The puffin, with a huff that ruffled his immaculate feathers, waddled over and, with an air of regal importance that would have made a king blush, settled onto Orla’s shoulder. He nudged her cheek with his beak, a gesture that spoke volumes of his earned, if grudging, trust. He hadn’t sought rescue; he had sought an audience, and Orla, by simply being there with quiet understanding and a willingness to understand his particular brand of puffin logic, had provided it. He knew she wouldn’t scold him for his elaborate nesting choices, and that was worth a great deal.

Zephyr and Gale finally noticed them, their magical duel sputtering to a rather ignominious halt. “Who dares interrupt the symphony of spellcraft?” Zephyr demanded, his voice laced with indignant outrage.

Orla, with Percival preening ostentatiously on her shoulder, simply tilted her head, her spectacles glinting. “I believe your performance has concluded,” she said, her voice as calm as a frozen lake. “And,” she added, gesturing with a herb-smelling finger towards Percival’s nest, “your audience has found a more comfortable seat. It seems your discarded materials have proven quite… useful.”

Gale squinted at Percival, then at the elaborate nest. “He… he used our discarded glamour-dust to make a pillow? And our crystallised laughter for decoration?”

“It appears so,” Orla said dryly, a faint smile playing on her lips. “Quite an innovative use of materials, if I do say so myself. He has a very discerning eye for interior design.”

Pip, unable to resist, added, his voice a low chuckle, “That is not a prophecy. That is a shopping list with ambition. And a rather excellent understanding of comfort, I might add.”

Zephyr and Gale exchanged a look, a flicker of something akin to sheepishness crossing their flamboyant faces. They were undeniably skilled at magic, masters of dazzling displays and theatrical pronouncements. But perhaps, just perhaps, they weren’t quite as adept at understanding the quiet desires of a discerning puffin who valued comfort and a well-appointed nest above all else. Their grand magic had inadvertently provided Percival with his ultimate prize.

As they made their way back down the mountain, the wind combed through the prayer flags strung along the passes and whispered through the fir branches, carrying the faint receding echoes of Zephyr and Gale’s still-grumbling critiques of each other’s artistic merit. Percival, nestled contentedly on Orla’s shoulder, occasionally let out a soft happy chirrup, his beak occasionally nudging Orla’s ear as if sharing a secret only they understood. Cobble, for once, seemed to have forgotten to grumble, his steady hooves carrying them all homeward with a quiet contented rhythm. The sock drawer, when they got back, was still on the floor. Percival approved of that too.
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
